1:
The increase is stated without comment and the witnesses supply it. Clarke warns that the multiplying is not to be dated here at all, the writer speaking of what had happened long before. Keil takes it of the whole human race; Gill narrows it to the posterity of Cain, mere natural men destitute of the grace of God, who multiplied faster than Seth's line because polygamy had spread among them after Lamech's example. Ellicott argues the growth must have been slow, since each patriarch reached a great age before the son who is named, and that name is not necessarily the eldest but the one who held the birthright — Noah, born when his father was a hundred and eighty-two, perhaps with elder siblings unnamed; yet Cain could build a city, so a considerable population was already possible. Henry makes the increase itself the first cause of the wickedness: it was the effect of the blessing, and corruption so abused it that it turned into a curse. The more sinners the more sin, and the multitude of offenders emboldens men, as infectious diseases are deadliest in populous cities and sin is a spreading leprosy. Wesley keeps that sentence almost word for word.

Who the sons of God were is the question of the passage, and Keil sets out the three answers held from the earliest times: the sons of princes, angels, or the Sethites, with the daughters of men correspondingly of the lower orders, of mankind at large, or of the Cainites. Gill and Calvin reach the third by eliminating the others. Gill denies the angels because they are incorporeal and neither marry nor generate, and denies the nobles because marrying beneath oneself is no crime and could at most produce a partial rather than a universal corruption. Calvin is blunter: the ancient figment of intercourse between angels and women is refuted by its own absurdity, and it is surprising that learned men were ever fascinated by ravings so gross, while the Chaldee paraphrase, condemning marriages between the sons of nobles and the daughters of plebeians, is merely frigid. Ellicott alone turns the usual reading round. He grants the Sethite view is the one most accepted in modern times, then asks how the marriage of pious men to women of an inferior race could produce mighty men and men of renown; he insists the phrase conveys no idea of piety, the word constantly meaning mighty ones and being elsewhere rendered judges; and he argues that the daughters of men in the second verse must be those of the first, who were Sethites. On his reading the pious are the women, and the mighty the intruders.

What was wrong with the marriages is agreed in substance. Henry lists three faults: they chose only by the eye, seeing the women were fair, which was all they looked at; they followed their own corrupt affections without advice; and they were unequally yoked with unbelievers, a thing afterwards forbidden to Israel, which ruined Solomon and troubled the returned exiles. His maxim is that the bad will sooner debauch the good than the good reform the bad, and Wesley repeats the first fault in his very words. Calvin is careful to say what is not condemned: not that beauty was regarded in choosing a wife, nor is fornication the charge, but that mere lust reigned, marriage being too sacred a thing for men to be drawn into it by the lust of the eyes, since the union is inseparable and takes in every part of life. That they took of all they chose shows they sought no necessary endowments but wandered without discrimination. He treats the mingling itself as the graver matter, since the separation of God's worshippers from profane nations was a sacred appointment made so that a Church might exist on earth, and to confound that order was intolerable profanation.
3:
The contested verb in the third verse is settled differently by each. Keil takes it to mean rule, and to judge as the consequence of ruling, so the spirit is the divine principle of life which God will now withdraw, ending their course. Ellicott agrees the verb more exactly means to rule or preside, notes that the versions generally render it dwell or abide, and says the context fixes the sense whichever way one takes the spirit, as the animating breath or as conscience and moral sense: the struggle is not to be indefinitely prolonged. Calvin surveys the derivations and rejects one outright, that the word means a scabbard, so that God would no longer have his Spirit held captive in the body like a sword in its sheath — a reading he calls distorted and redolent of the Manichean delirium that the soul is a portion of the divine Spirit. Henry and Clarke read the striving as the Spirit's ordinary work on conscience: he strove by Noah's preaching and by inward checks, and where he is resisted and quenched, though he strive long he will not strive always, so that those he has left off striving with are ripening for ruin. On the reason given, Henry takes for that he also is flesh to mean incurably corrupt, so that striving is labour lost, and asks whether the Ethiopian can change his skin; Wesley condenses him closely.

The hundred and twenty years divides them. Clarke and Wesley take it for a reprieve: the earth was already ripe for destruction, but a respite was granted in which repentance was possible, and Wesley dramatises it, justice saying cut them down and mercy interceding to let them alone this year also, mercy prevailing so far as to obtain six score years. Ellicott denies that reading altogether. The whole purpose of the verse, he says, is a divine determination to shorten human life, reducing its extreme duration to what might still be its normal length under the most favourable conditions, so that the number is the new span of a life and not a countdown to the flood. Keil stands with him, since on his reading the withdrawal of the spirit is what ends the long lives. Neither side disputes the arithmetic; they disagree about what is being measured, a delay or a lifetime. Gill adds that the saying was spoken by God within himself rather than to Noah, who has not yet been mentioned; Ellicott presses that the man addressed is the adam of the previous verses, meant especially of the Sethites.

On the Nephilim almost everyone rejects the giants of the English. Clarke derives the word from a root meaning to fall and takes them for those fallen from the true religion, complains that the Greek rendering, which literally means earth-born, gave us giants without regard to the sense, and observes that our translators used that one word for seven different Hebrew ones. Keil follows Luther in rendering them tyrants, so called because they fell upon the people and oppressed them, and reports that Luther rejected the giant sense as fabulous. Calvin canvasses the etymologies, that they exceeded the common stature, that men's countenances fell at the sight of them, that all fell prostrate in terror, and prefers a figure from a torrent or tempest: as a storm falling violently lays waste the fields, so these robbers laid waste the world. Moses, he insists, calls them robust and not tall, distinguishing them by their rapine and lust of dominion. Gill offers the same options and prefers apostasy, which he thinks much better than the Targum's apostate angels, whom it even names. Ellicott alone defends the stature, thinking an age of long lives likely to produce a taller race, and cites Lenormant for a root meaning to be wonderful, compared with an Assyrian word for an ogre unique in size.
5:
The indictment is drawn in two stages and the witnesses follow both. Gill and Calvin stress the extent first: the corruption had spread through Cain's line and Seth's alike, now mixed into one people, so integrity possessed no longer a single corner; and Calvin concludes that the earth was not overwhelmed with a deluge of waters until it had first been drowned in the pollution of wickedness. Then they go inward. Calvin says Moses traces the flood to outward acts and then ascends higher, finding the evil too deeply seated to leave hope of repentance; Clarke itemises the same descent: the men were flesh and wholly sensual, religion had neither science nor practice left, and the very first embryo of every idea was evil, the fountain itself incurably poisoned. Ellicott glosses the word rendered imagination as form or shape, so every embodied thought thrown up by the heart was evil all the day, without reproof of conscience or fear of justice; tracing the whole to the collapse of moral and social restraint. Wesley adds that the sins were not committed through carelessness but deliberately, men contriving how to do mischief. Keil turns the verse against the angel theory: a race so begotten would not be the race created in Adam, but a grotesque product.

That it repented the Lord is the difficulty, and four answer it the same way. Gill calls it an anthropopathy and gives the figure: as a potter who has made a vessel that does not please him repents of it and breaks it in pieces, so God resolved to destroy what he had made. Henry insists the words cannot reflect on God's immutability, since nothing can disturb the Eternal Mind; they express his just displeasure, and his image is of a man wronged by those he was kind to, who repents of his kindness and wishes he had never fostered the snake that now hisses in his face. Wesley follows him almost exactly, adding the neat formula that the change was in man, not in God. Calvin puts it most strongly: repentance cannot take place in God, since nothing happens to him unforeseen, and he is never sorrowful but remains in his own happy repose; the Spirit accommodates himself to our capacity, and the words teach that God will no longer own the creature as his workmanship or as the man formed in his image. Ellicott alone declines that approach and frames it as an antinomy: sovereignty and human freedom must both be true though we cannot combine them, Scripture keeping the second in the foreground because responsibility depends on it.

The sentence reaches the animals, which troubles them. Calvin admits it looks like exceeding moderation, since neither asses nor oxen had done evil, and answers that creatures made for man's sake and living by his use were drawn into his ruin when he fell. Ellicott reads the verb as delete or rub out and limits the scope: the text says the destruction reaches to the beasts, not that every animal perished, and wild beasts go unmentioned probably because the domestic cattle would suffer most. Wesley gives the verb three pictures: dirt wiped from a place that should be clean, lines blotted from a book that displease the author, a citizen's name struck from the rolls when he is disfranchised. Then the chapter turns. Ellicott notes this is the first mention of grace in the Bible, and that the purpose was never extermination but regeneration. Calvin warns against supposing Noah found grace by his own industry, since his integrity itself came of preventing mercy; Gill says the same, that God always reserves a remnant, owing to grace and not to merit. Clarke gives the three grounds the text supplies, that Noah was just, perfect in his generation and walked with God; Henry observes that finding one good man vindicates the verdict on all the rest.
9:
The heading is read two ways. Gill takes the generations of Noah for the account of his posterity, the genealogy of the new world beginning where the old ends at the flood, but records that Aben Ezra and Ben Gersom render the word events, the things that befell him. Calvin agrees the word properly means generation but has a wider use covering the whole history of a life, which he thinks the sense here, since what follows is a description of the man rather than a list. On that description they are careful. Ellicott insists that perfect means sound or healthy and conveys no idea of sinlessness, answering to the Latin integer, whence our word integrity, and not to perfectus; and that generations in the second half of the verse is a different word from the first, meaning simply his contemporaries. Keil says the same, glossing the phrase as the families that passed by Noah, the Nestor of his time, and finds the proof of his righteousness in his walking with God, as Enoch had. Wesley makes the righteousness forensic before it is practical, Noah justified by faith in the promised seed and then righteous in conversation; and he adds that it is easy to be religious when religion is in fashion, but strong faith to swim against the stream when no one else appears for God.

The two charges are taken in order. Corrupt before God is referred by Gill, Henry and Wesley to worship: either they had other gods, or worshipped him by images, or, as Henry puts it, were corrupt in contempt of God, daring him and defying him to his face; Gill cites Jarchi for uncleanness and idolatry together. Filled with violence is referred to men, and Henry describes a world with no order nor regular government, where no man was safe in what he had the clearest right to, not even in life, but there was nothing but murders and rapine. His moral is that wickedness ruins human society as well as shaming human nature, since take away conscience and the fear of God and men become beasts and devils to one another. Calvin makes the same two clauses cause and effect: the light of equity being extinct, men who have revolted from God forget mutual equity and are carried into insane ferocity. Ellicott notices that the larger word for earth is used six times in three verses, and limits it: not the whole material globe, but so much of it as man, and notably the mighty men, had filled with violence.

On the last verse the question is how far flesh reaches. Keil argues it cannot include the animals here, since to have corrupted one's way can be said of man only; and he meets the objection that later verses use the phrase of beasts by noting that a few verses on it means the animals alone, so the sense must be fixed each time by context. Calvin takes the word in this place as neutral, standing for mankind without censure, as when all flesh is said to see the glory of the Lord. Ellicott goes the other way and implicates the things themselves: incapable of good or evil, they had been made instruments of man's carnal will, and the associations they had acquired were reason enough to rub them out. Gill and Wesley dwell on the looking rather than the flesh. Gill notes it is said as though God had never looked before, whereas his eye is always on the earth, so the word marks special notice and the behold marks certainty, the omniscient God having declared it; Wesley says he was an eye-witness, and that the wickedness was not of some particular nations but of the whole world, there being none good beside Noah. Clarke passes the section over, referring back to his note on the earlier verse.
13:
The sentence is announced to Noah before it falls, and the phrasing is worked over. Ellicott hears a court metaphor in the end of all flesh is come before me, the decree laid before the sovereign for his sign manual; the verb rendered destroy, he notes, is not the one used earlier but the one translated corrupted, and with the earth should be even the earth, so that what is brought to nothing is the whole present constitution of things. Keil gets there another way: the idiom means to reach the ear, so the end spoken of is not destruction but the extremity of corruption that leads to it; and he marks the talion, that flesh which had destroyed its way is destroyed with the earth. Clarke takes destroying the earth for an alteration of its very constitution. Henry makes the telling itself a mercy: God makes Noah the man of his counsel, as he afterwards told Abraham of Sodom. Calvin observes that the warning was meant to frighten as well as comfort, since while life seemed secure Noah would never have laboured at the ark as he did.

On the vessel they agree it was no ship. Gill insists it is called an ark or chest because it was never meant to sail, only to float, and notes that Lucian and other heathen writers call it a chest. Ellicott says the word is so archaic that scholars know neither its derivation nor its language, and draws a sharp inference: the Chaldean account of the flood speaks throughout like a maritime people, while this history is plainly the work of a people living inland. Clarke adds that the word is used only of this and of the vessel in which Moses was hidden, and means no more than our word vessel, a hollow thing of no fixed shape. On the wood, Gill lists the guesses of the Targums and rabbins — cedar, box, pine, fir — and settles with Clarke, Ellicott and Keil on cypress, for the sound of the word and because the timber resists rot and worm and was used anciently in shipbuilding; Clarke observes that the ancient versions plainly did not know, rendering it square or planed timber, while the Syriac and Arabic trifle with it as wicker, as if the ark were a great basket. The rooms are literally nests, which Ellicott takes for cells in three tiers whose interlacing timbers helped hold the whole together; the pitch is bitumen.

The measurements divide them only over the cubit. Ellicott takes it at eighteen inches, a quarter of a man's height, making the ark four hundred and fifty feet by seventy-five by forty-five, and remarks that a hull so long would be hard to build for fear of breaking her back. Clarke prefers Greaves, who measured the pyramids and made the ancient cubit nearly twenty-two inches, stretching the ark to five hundred and forty-seven feet. Calvin reports the older difficulty, that profane men ridiculed the size as too small for the creatures, Origen answering with a geometrical cubit six times the common, Augustine assenting. The window puzzles them more. Gill and Clarke both report the rabbinic notion of a luminous stone from the Pison hung like a chandelier, and both prefer an opening, Clarke taking the word collectively for apertures of light and air. Ellicott and Keil make ventilation the point: the word is the singular of the term for midday, and since the hull was pitched inside and out the lower storeys would serve only for stores, so they read an open space a cubit deep under the eaves. Wesley draws the lesson that God could have preserved Noah by angels without any pains of his own, but chose to employ him, for the trial of his faith and to teach that none are saved but such as work out their salvation.
17:
The word for the flood is peculiar to it. Clarke and Keil both note it is used of this event only, Keil calling it archaic and coined for the waters of Noah, Clarke inferring that no other flood was ever like it, there having been many partial inundations but only one general deluge, with a promise of no second. How far it reached divides them sharply. Gill marshals the heathen testimony for a universal flood: every nation kept the story but put its own ancient worthy in Noah's place, the Greeks Deucalion or Ogyges; he cites Josephus for Berosus, and Eusebius for Melo, who wrote against the Jews and yet reports the deluge. Ellicott argues the opposite, that the words about all things dying by no means require a universal deluge; following Tayler Lewis, he holds the writer described faithfully what he had seen or received, and that we may not force on him our modern knowledge of the earth, its Alps and Himalayas and round figure, far beyond anything he could conceive; unnecessary miracle, he adds, is contrary to the wisdom of God. Wesley leaves the compass alone and presses the pronoun: I who am infinite in power can do it, and infinite in justice will.

The covenant is the first named in the book, and each takes it his own way. Ellicott makes it the beginning of a new order: there had been none with Adam or the Sethites, but from Noah man holds a more exactly defined relation to God, of which revelation is the necessary result, two contracting parties needing to communicate. He adds that this is why our Bible is called a Testament, the Greek word being wider than ours, covering both an agreement between the living and the instrument by which a man disposes of his goods at death. Clarke goes to the etymology and finds a root meaning to purify, since God could enter no covenant without a purifier, so the same word serves for the covenant and for the sacrifice that ratified it, and is applied to Christ; he describes the rite, the victim divided in two and the parties passing between the halves. Gill takes the promise concretely: Noah kept from the rage of wicked men while he built, saved in the ark, and made to repeople the world. Wesley calls it the covenant of providence, that nature's course should continue notwithstanding the interruption. Calvin explains why it comes here: the work was long and hard, and a command is freely embraced only when a promise is joined to it.

On the creatures they add little. Clarke observes that God might have destroyed the animals and made new ones, but chose to preserve what he had, though it took more contrivance to save the old than to make others, nothing being wantonly wasted. Calvin makes the two and two a figure rather than a count, since more of the clean kinds went in; only breeding pairs being mentioned, the number is not stated but the sexes coupled, that Noah might see how the world was to be replenished. The last verse draws out the rest. Henry lists the objections Noah might have raised: that the God who made the world should so soon unmake it, that he who drew the waters off the land should let them cover it again, whence water enough could come, and why the warning came to him alone. His faith triumphed over all of them. Calvin dwells on the labour, the trees to be felled and joined, the work stretching past a hundred years, and the certainty that his neighbours would not bear with a man promising himself an exclusive deliverance. Clarke adds that he preached righteousness all that while; Gill, that in his fear, faith and obedience he was a type of the church's builder.
